notes: Table 1 / Appendix A.4 give the final cohort's sensitive-attribute distribution with no pre-filter denominator, so neither reading is satisfied. Insurance has an explicit UNKNOWN level that is retained and analysed (994 train / 192 test), hence separate_category.

HARD CASE (minor): the only reported denominator-like comparison is between subgroup TPR disparity and subgroup proportional disease membership within the final datasets - that is a within-pool model analysis, not a retention comparison, so both readings are 'no'. null_attribute_handling: the standard absence search (missing/unknown/not reported/declined/imputation/complete case) returns 0 hits, but the Data section states race/insurance are available 'excluding around 100,000 images', which I read as those images being dropped from the race/insurance analyses. Judgement call; 'reports_only' is the plausible alternative.

HARD CASE. The paper repeatedly says groups are 'underrepresented in the selected set', but 'selected set' means the model's predicted-positive set (Equal Parity / Proportional Parity), not the analysis cohort - this is a model audit, not a selection audit, so strict = no. For the permissive column: the Data section gives MIMIC-III parent demographics (about 69% White) and Table III gives the final cohort group size ratios (White 0.69), but the paper never juxtaposes or compares them, and the only representativeness statement ('a subset of data ... not entirely representative of the overall population') cites no figure, which the rule explicitly excludes. Coded literal = no. null_attribute_handling: 'other/unknown' appears only as a listed MIMIC insurance value; the analysis insurance groups contain no unknown level and no handling is stated, so unclear.

cohort_is_filtered is a judgement call: the authors take all 10,000 Harvard-FairVLMed samples but construct the benchmark themselves and apply an LLM self-check post-processing step, which the protocol's benchmark-curation note treats as filtering. No source-population or external figure is compared to the benchmark's demographic composition, so both selection readings are no.

HARD CASE (near miss). MENTAT is a clinician-authored vignette benchmark in which patient demographics are assigned at random, so there is no patient selection step at all. The closest thing to a selection audit is an annotator-bias check (whether annotation behaviour differs by the gender coding of the question), which tests the labellers rather than the retention of patients, so it does not qualify under either reading. cohort_is_filtered coded yes on the analysis-set narrowing to three task categories for the free-form evaluation.

HARD CASE - the decisive disagreement candidate. The authors deliberately drew a skin-tone-balanced sample of 600 cases from SCIN, and Appendix 1 reports the SCIN parent distribution numerically (Type I 7.5% ... Type VI 5.7%) alongside the statement that darker tones are underrepresented in SCIN. Strict = no because the retained cohort's composition is described only qualitatively ('balanced'), no retention rate by group is given, and the two figures are never juxtaposed or tested. Permissive = yes because specific parent-database group figures are reported and set against the authors' own balanced selection, which is exactly what 'comparing cohort demographics to the full parent database before the authors' filtering' covers.

HARD CASE. The paper reports, for each protected attribute, the analysis cohort size against the pre-filter reviewed-case denominator N=7,166 (Sex 6,505; Age 6,786; Race 920; SES 1,929) and Table 3 gives each group's frequency as a percentage of that same N=7,166 with an explicit Missing row (Race Missing 86.9%). That is an inclusion rate reported against a pre-selection denominator, which is why I coded the permissive column yes. Strict = no because the missingness is never disaggregated by group within an attribute - you cannot tell from anything reported whether, say, non-White patients were more likely to have race undocumented - so no test or comparison of differential retention across groups exists. A first coder who reads Table 3's percentages as 'percent retained by group relative to the pre-filter cohort' would code strict = yes; I judged that the group-level differential retention question is untestable here and therefore untested.

HARD CASE. Table I compares the NHANES development cohort's demographic composition against the BRFSS national survey sample with p-values (e.g. Male 48.5% vs 46.4%, p<0.001). That is a comparison of cohort group composition to an external, nationally representative figure, so the permissive reading is satisfied - even though the authors' intent is distribution-shift assessment for external validation, not representativeness. Strict = no: neither cohort is compared to its own pre-filter denominator and no retention rate by group is reported. null_attribute_handling is internally contradictory in the paper: the NHANES cohort is restricted to participants with 'complete information on predictors' (a complete-case rule) while preprocessing says missing categorical values were mode-imputed; I coded imputes on the explicit imputation sentence and flag the conflict.

Near-total population cohort (all California live births 2011-2017). A single overall linkage rate (98.2%) is reported but never disaggregated by group, and the only external figure ('California is a diverse state that represents 1 in 8 births in the U.S.') describes the state rather than the cohort's group composition, so both readings are no.

37,493 eligible surgical patients reduce to a final cohort of 14,263 via a CONSORT-style flow figure (Figure 2) that gives counts only, with no demographic breakdown of those excluded - exactly the case the protocol says does not qualify. The representativeness claim in the limitations cites no figure. null_attribute_handling coded imputes on a statement that covers missing variables generically (the protected attributes race, language, health literacy, insurance and ADI are among the model variables); the detail is in an unavailable supplement, so this is the weakest of my null codes.

Cohort selection is presented as a flow figure (Figure 1) with counts only. The >97% coverage figure is a total, not by group. Maryland and Florida are described as differing in racial and ethnic distribution, but no state or census composition figure is ever set against the cohort's, so the permissive reading is not met either.

Clear split between the two readings. The Methods state the health system's served (catchment) population composition with specific figures (52% NHB, 29% H, 9% NHW) and the paper elsewhere reports the analytic sample as 54% Black, 27% Latina - the catchment comparison the permissive column is designed to capture. Nothing compares the retained cohort to the pre-exclusion EMR extract, and no retention rate by group is given, so strict = no.

Exclusion counts (61 / 1,562 / 5,519 from 119,131) are given as totals with no demographic breakdown - flow-diagram-equivalent, so no under the strict rule. The 18% of the retained cohort with race not recorded is reported and analysed as its own Unknown/Not Reported group, which is separate_category, not drops. The only external referent (NSQIP underrepresenting small hospitals) is about hospitals, not patient group composition.

Patients who declined to report race or ethnicity are folded into analysed 'Other' and 'Not Hispanic or Latino' categories rather than dropped, hence separate_category. A catchment area is described but never quantified demographically, and Table 1 is a straightforward final-cohort description, so both selection readings are no.

HARD CASE (permissive column only). The Results state 'The sample was reflective of an urban, adult primary care population' - a representativeness claim, but it attaches a citation rather than a numeric external figure, and the protocol explicitly excludes representativeness statements with no figure. Coded literal = no on that basis. No enrolment/refusal counts are reported at all, so nothing about differential recruitment can be assessed. Participants with unknown race are retained in an analysed 'Other, multiple, or unknown' category.

HARD CASE (thematic near miss). The entire paper is about detecting dataset-level 'sampling bias', which sounds like a selection audit, but the operationalisation (AEq learning-curve values compared between groups on the same label) never invokes a pre-selection population denominator or a retention rate - it compares subgroup learnability inside the assembled dataset. The one sentence that gestures at a source comparison ('a dataset reflecting the underlying empirical group frequencies') gives no figure, which the permissive rule excludes. Coded no under both readings.

HARD CASE. Table 2 lists the 280 Medicare/VA patients excluded from the socioeconomic analysis (58.2%) beside the retained Advantaged (21.8%) and Disadvantaged (20.0%) groups, all as percentages of the same 481-patient cohort - formally a retained-versus-excluded breakdown. I coded both readings no because the excluded stratum is defined by the socioeconomic attribute itself (so no differential-retention question across groups is even posed), nothing is compared for race or marital status, and there is no external or parent-database referent. A coder treating Table 2 as 'percent retained by group relative to the pre-filter cohort' could reach yes on the permissive column.

Missingness per variable is reported (0.02% to 16.5%, income worst) and then mode-imputed, so imputes rather than reports_only. The restriction is on the outcome variable, not on the protected attributes. Survey weights are applied to represent the Tennessee adult population, and the prevalence estimate is benchmarked against a Kaiser Family Foundation figure - but that is an outcome benchmark, not a comparison of the cohort's group composition to an external figure, so the permissive reading is not met.

21,837 PTB-XL recordings are reduced to 21,507 by an age cut and a signal-quality filter, with no demographic breakdown of what was dropped. The PTB-XL sex balance (47.5%/52.5%) is stated for the source dataset but is never set against the retained cohort's composition, so I read it as dataset description rather than a comparison; permissive = no. Missing demographics are explicitly imputed (population/sex-stratified means, s=0.5), hence imputes.
